items.title: Ad click aggregator system map
items.purpose: Establish the component map and the two-consumer split before any mechanism sheet goes deep.
items.description: One durable log feeds two consumers: a stream job for freshness and a raw archive for the nightly batch that produces the number you invoice on.

flow.title: Collect and batch
flow.detail: Ad servers emit clicks to a collector that validates, enriches and batches into the log.

flow.title: Partition by ad_id
flow.detail: Every event for one ad lands on one partition so aggregation uses local state, never a shuffle.

flow.title: Aggregate in event time
flow.detail: The stream job keeps per-ad windowed counters in checkpointed state and emits completed minutes.

flow.title: Archive and reconcile
flow.detail: A parallel sink writes raw events to object storage; a nightly batch recomputes and overwrites finalized periods.

flow.title: Serve precomputed rollups
flow.detail: The query service reads only (ad_id, minute) rollups — never raw events.

numbers.label: Write volume
numbers.detail: ~11.5K events/sec average, designed for ~50K/sec peak.

numbers.label: Raw retention
numbers.detail: ~150 bytes per event; cheap in object storage, too much to keep hot.

numbers.label: Freshness target
numbers.detail: Near-real-time, not real-time — the watermark slack is the dial.

priorities: Correctness good enough to bill on
tradeoffs: Stream layer gives freshness but is approximate under failure
Batch layer gives truth but lags by hours
Two aggregation implementations can drift — alert on the delta

items.title: Event time, watermarks and late events
items.purpose: Show why the bucket a click lands in is decided by when it happened, not when it arrived.
items.description: A window closes when the watermark passes its end. Allowed lateness buys a correction; anything later goes to a side output the batch layer reconciles.

flow.title: Stamp event time
flow.detail: The click carries the time it happened; processing time is only when the aggregator saw it.

flow.title: Advance the watermark
flow.detail: Watermark = max observed event time minus slack, declaring "all events up to T are believed seen".

flow.title: Close the window
flow.detail: When the watermark passes a window end, the window emits its value.

flow.title: Accept late corrections
flow.detail: Within allowed lateness a straggler updates the window and re-emits a corrected number.

flow.title: Divert the very late
flow.detail: Beyond that, events go to a side output — never to the floor.

numbers.label: Watermark slack
numbers.detail: The explicit latency-versus-completeness dial.

numbers.label: Window grain
numbers.detail: Minutes roll asynchronously into hours and days.

priorities: Explicit late policy over silent drops
tradeoffs: More slack means later results but fewer late events
Less slack means fresher numbers but more corrections
Processing time is simpler but reassigns revenue during lag spikes

items.title: Two-stage aggregation for a whale advertiser
items.purpose: Make it obvious that adding partitions cannot split a single key, and show the shape that can.
items.description: One advertiser at 40% of traffic saturates a single partition. Salting the key into sub-keys spreads it across partitions at the cost of a merge stage.

flow.title: Detect the skew
flow.detail: Per-partition throughput — not the healthy aggregate — reveals the hot key.

flow.title: Salt the key
flow.detail: ad_42 becomes ad_42:0..N, so one logical key hashes to many partitions.

flow.title: Aggregate in parallel
flow.detail: Each salted bucket keeps its own local counter on its own consumer.

flow.title: Merge in stage two
flow.detail: A second aggregation sums the salted buckets back into one (ad_id, minute) value.

numbers.label: Skew example
numbers.detail: A single campaign can dominate the entire firehose.

numbers.label: Salt width
numbers.detail: Wide enough to spread, narrow enough to keep the merge cheap.

priorities: Bounded merge cost over unbounded skew
Generalized fix over per-advertiser special cases
tradeoffs: Salting adds a second aggregation stage and latency
More partitions alone cannot split one hash value
A dedicated cluster per whale does not generalize

items.title: Why a crash does not double-count
items.purpose: Show the precise crash window and the two properties that close it.
items.description: Offsets and sink writes commit in one transaction, and windows are written as absolute upserts — so a replay overwrites rather than increments.

flow.title: Checkpoint state and offsets
flow.detail: The processor snapshots keyed state together with its source position.

flow.title: Process a batch
flow.detail: Counters advance in local state; nothing is durable yet.

flow.title: Crash before commit
flow.detail: On restart the job restores the checkpoint and replays from that exact offset.

flow.title: Commit atomically
flow.detail: Source offsets and sink writes land in a single transaction, so there is no gap or overlap.

flow.title: Upsert absolute values
flow.detail: Writing the window total rather than a delta makes any replay idempotent.

numbers.label: Delivery guarantee
numbers.detail: The log redelivers; the state transition is what happens once.

numbers.label: Checkpoint interval
numbers.detail: Longer intervals mean cheaper steady state and slower recovery.

tradeoffs: Transactional sinks add coordination latency
Long checkpoints destabilize recovery
Exactly-once covers internal state, never external side effects

design-problems/p19.summary: Four sheets separate the topic-and-consumer-group map from the storage layout, the replication protocol, and the failover decision that trades data for availability.

items.title: Message queue system map
items.purpose: Establish that a topic is a set of independently ordered partitions read by independent consumer groups.
items.description: Producers hash keys to partitions; each consumer group tracks its own offsets, so groups read the same data at their own pace without interfering.

flow.title: Hash the key
flow.detail: hash(key) % partitions picks the partition, which is what preserves per-key ordering.

flow.title: Append to the log
flow.detail: The partition leader appends to a segmented, append-only file.

flow.title: Replicate to followers
flow.detail: Followers pull from the leader exactly like ordinary consumers.

flow.title: Track offsets per group
flow.detail: The broker holds one offset per group per partition, not per-message ack state.

flow.title: Retain by time or size
flow.detail: Messages are not deleted on read, which is what makes replay and multiple groups possible.

numbers.label: Target throughput
numbers.detail: ~1 GB/sec at 1 KB average, 3 GB/sec written at RF=3.

numbers.label: Retention
numbers.detail: ~600 TB replicated — retention is a design decision, not a config afterthought.

numbers.label: Broker sustained write
numbers.detail: Sequential; network usually binds before disk does.

priorities: Horizontal partition scaling over vertical broker scaling
tradeoffs: Global ordering would cap throughput at one machine
Each extra consumer group re-reads the topic, multiplying egress
Partition count is a hard ceiling on a group’s parallelism

items.title: Partition storage: segments and the sparse index
items.purpose: Show why a disk-backed log outruns an in-memory queue.
items.description: Appends are sequential into fixed-size segment files; a sparse offset index turns a seek into a binary search plus a short scan, and expiry is a file unlink.

flow.title: Append to the open segment
flow.detail: Only the newest segment accepts writes; older ones are immutable.

flow.title: Index sparsely
flow.detail: An offset-to-byte index per segment avoids scanning the file to find a position.

flow.title: Serve reads from page cache
flow.detail: Trailing reads hit the OS page cache rather than the disk.

flow.title: Send without copying
flow.detail: sendfile pushes pages straight to the socket, never entering application memory.

flow.title: Expire whole segments
flow.detail: Retention deletes files instead of compacting rows.

numbers.label: Segment size
numbers.detail: Bounds index size and makes expiry coarse and cheap.

numbers.label: Copy count
numbers.detail: The broker never transforms the payload, so it never has to materialize it.

priorities: Page cache over an application-managed cache
tradeoffs: Immutability means space is reclaimed only at segment granularity
Zero-copy is lost the moment the broker must transform payloads
Cold reads that miss page cache fall back to disk latency

items.title: Leader, followers and the in-sync replica set
items.purpose: Make the commit rule and the acks dial concrete.
items.description: A record is committed once it reaches every in-sync replica, and consumers read only up to that high-water mark — so a failover can never erase a record a consumer already saw.

flow.title: Write to the leader
flow.detail: All reads and writes for a partition go to its leader.

flow.title: Followers fetch
flow.detail: Followers replicate by pulling, and fall out of the ISR when they lag.

flow.title: Commit at the ISR
flow.detail: The high-water mark is the minimum offset present on every in-sync replica.

flow.title: Gate consumer reads
flow.detail: Consumers cannot read past the high-water mark.

flow.title: Acknowledge per policy
flow.detail: acks=0, 1 or all decides how much of this the producer waits for.

numbers.label: Replication factor
numbers.detail: Two follower copies; survives one broker loss with room to spare.

numbers.label: min.insync.replicas
numbers.detail: Without this, acks=all silently degrades to acks=1 as the ISR shrinks.

priorities: Explicit producer control over hidden defaults
tradeoffs: acks=all costs latency on every write
acks=1 loses data if the leader dies before followers catch up
A shrunk ISR weakens guarantees without any error being raised

items.title: Leader failure and the unclean-election choice
items.purpose: Present the availability-versus-durability decision as a decision, not a default.
items.description: Electing from the ISR preserves every committed record. Electing outside it restores availability by accepting data loss — which is a policy choice someone must make deliberately.

flow.title: Detect the failure
flow.detail: The controller notices the leader is gone.

flow.title: Check the ISR
flow.detail: If any in-sync replica survives, elect from it and lose nothing committed.

flow.title: Face the empty ISR
flow.detail: If none survives, the partition is unavailable until one returns.

flow.title: Decide unclean election
flow.detail: Allowing a stale replica to lead restores writes and discards committed records.

numbers.label: Clean election loss
numbers.detail: The high-water mark guarantees the new leader has them all.

numbers.label: Unclean election loss
numbers.detail: Whatever the stale replica never received is gone.

priorities: Explicit operator choice over silent degradation
tradeoffs: Refusing unclean election means accepting downtime
Allowing it means acknowledged writes can vanish
Aggressive failure detection risks flapping leadership

design-problems/p21.title: Distributed Key-Value Store visual study set
design-problems/p21.summary: Four sheets separate the masterless system map from ring placement, the quorum overlap argument, and the three repair mechanisms that make leaderless writes converge.

items.title: Key-value store system map
items.purpose: Establish that any node can coordinate, and that no node is special.
items.description: The ring decides placement, gossip keeps membership current, and every node runs the same LSM engine — so there is no master to lose.

flow.title: Accept anywhere
flow.detail: Any node can act as coordinator for any request.

flow.title: Look up the ring
flow.detail: hash(key) walks clockwise to its owner and the next distinct physical replicas.

flow.title: Fan out to the preference list
flow.detail: The coordinator writes to W replicas and reads from R.

flow.title: Store in an LSM engine
flow.detail: Writes append to a commit log and a memtable, flushing to immutable SSTables.

flow.title: Gossip membership
flow.detail: Nodes swap state with random peers, spreading liveness without a coordinator.

numbers.label: Replication factor
numbers.detail: Survives one node loss with quorum intact.

numbers.label: Sizing example
numbers.detail: 300 TB replicated, ~450 TB provisioned once compaction headroom is included.

numbers.label: Virtual nodes
numbers.detail: Smooths ownership and parallelizes rebuild across many peers.

tradeoffs: Leaderless writes mean replicas diverge by design
AP posture rules out globally strict read-after-write
Tiny interface buys scale but forbids joins and multi-key transactions

items.title: Ring placement with virtual nodes
items.purpose: Show why membership change moves ~1/N of keys instead of nearly all of them.
items.description: Keys and nodes hash onto one ring. A key belongs to the first node clockwise; replicas are the next distinct physical nodes, skipping vnodes on a machine already chosen.

flow.title: Hash onto the ring
flow.detail: Both keys and virtual nodes occupy positions on a fixed hash space.

flow.title: Walk clockwise
flow.detail: The first vnode past the key’s hash is its coordinator.

flow.title: Skip duplicates
flow.detail: Replica selection skips vnodes mapping to a physical node or rack already in the list.

flow.title: Rebalance narrowly
flow.detail: A join or leave reassigns only the affected arc, not the whole keyspace.

numbers.label: Keys moved on change
numbers.detail: Versus nearly 100% with hash(key) % node_count.

numbers.label: Vnodes per node
numbers.detail: More vnodes means smoother ownership and faster parallel rebuild.

priorities: Rack and AZ diversity within the preference list
tradeoffs: More vnodes means more metadata and gossip state
Skipping duplicates complicates replica selection
Without the skip, three replicas can silently be one machine

items.title: Why R + W > N works
items.purpose: Reduce the quorum rule to the pigeonhole argument a candidate can redraw from memory.
items.description: If writes land on W replicas and reads consult R, and R + W exceeds N, the sets must share a node — so a read always sees at least one copy of the newest acknowledged write.

flow.title: Write to W replicas
flow.detail: The write is acknowledged once W members confirm.

flow.title: Read from R replicas
flow.detail: The coordinator gathers R responses and compares versions.

flow.title: Force an overlap
flow.detail: R + W > N guarantees at least one replica appears in both sets.

flow.title: Resolve by version
flow.detail: The newest version wins, and read repair pushes it to the stale replicas.

numbers.label: Typical setting
numbers.detail: Overlap of one, tolerating a single replica being down on each path.

numbers.label: Fast-read variant
numbers.detail: Cheapest reads, most expensive and least available writes.

tradeoffs: Higher W means more durable writes and worse write availability
Higher R means safer reads and higher read latency
Overlap does not mean all replicas are current — only that one is

items.title: Three repair mechanisms on three timescales
items.purpose: Show that no single repair mechanism is sufficient, and which one covers cold data.
items.description: Read repair fixes what is read, hinted handoff covers brief outages, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy is the only mechanism that ever repairs data nobody touches.

flow.title: Repair on read
flow.detail: A quorum read compares versions and asynchronously pushes the newest to stale replicas.

flow.title: Hold a hint
flow.detail: If a replica is briefly down, a peer accepts the write and replays it on recovery.

flow.title: Compare Merkle roots
flow.detail: Replicas exchange a hash tree over a key range; equal roots mean the range is in sync.

flow.title: Descend only where they differ
flow.detail: Unequal subtrees are walked down to isolate the differing keys.

flow.title: Sync the differing keys
flow.detail: Only those keys move, not the whole range.

numbers.label: Merkle comparison cost
numbers.detail: Locating differences costs a few exchanges, not a full range stream.

numbers.label: Tombstone lifetime
numbers.detail: Collect a delete marker too early and an offline replica resurrects the value.

priorities: Coverage of cold as well as hot data
tradeoffs: Read repair never touches data nobody reads
Hinted handoff helps only for transient failures
Anti-entropy costs background CPU and network continuously

design-problems/p22.title: LLM Inference Platform visual study set
design-problems/p22.summary: Four sheets separate the serving map from the three mechanisms that decide GPU economics: continuous batching, paged KV cache, and prefill/decode interference.

items.title: LLM inference platform system map
items.purpose: Establish that admission is gated on GPU memory, not on worker count.
items.description: Requests queue by priority and are admitted only when free KV blocks exist — because the real capacity unit is cache memory, not connections.

flow.title: Authenticate and route
flow.detail: The gateway applies auth, rate limits and model routing.

flow.title: Queue by priority
flow.detail: Interactive chat and offline batch occupy separate classes.

flow.title: Admit on free blocks
flow.detail: The scheduler admits a sequence only when KV cache capacity exists for it.

flow.title: Prefill then decode
flow.detail: The prompt is processed in parallel, then tokens are generated one step at a time.

flow.title: Stream and release
flow.detail: Tokens stream to the client; finishing or disconnecting frees blocks immediately.

numbers.label: Model weights
numbers.detail: 70B parameters at 2 bytes — tensor parallelism across GPUs is mandatory.

numbers.label: KV per token
numbers.detail: With grouped-query attention; roughly 8x larger without it.

numbers.label: Concurrent sequences
numbers.detail: 4K-token sequences in ~160 GB of leftover memory on a 4x80 GB node.

tradeoffs: Bigger batches raise throughput and worsen per-user latency
GPU autoscaling takes minutes, so headroom is mandatory
Long-context requests displace many ordinary ones

items.title: Static versus continuous batching
items.purpose: Show where the wasted GPU time goes in the naive design.
items.description: Output lengths vary by orders of magnitude, so static batches idle on finished sequences. Re-evaluating every decode step retires and admits continuously, so slots never sit empty.

flow.title: Admit a static batch
flow.detail: N requests start together and the batch returns together.

flow.title: Watch short ones idle
flow.detail: A sequence finishing at token 20 holds its slot until the longest finishes.

flow.title: Re-evaluate each step
flow.detail: Continuous batching inspects the batch after every decode step.

flow.title: Retire and admit
flow.detail: Finished sequences free their blocks and queued requests join immediately.

numbers.label: Length spread
numbers.detail: Utilization in a static batch trends toward average/maximum length.

numbers.label: Scheduling grain
numbers.detail: The finer the grain, the shorter the queueing delay.

tradeoffs: Per-step scheduling costs CPU overhead on the critical path
Larger batches improve throughput but raise per-user TPOT
Admission must be memory-aware or the batch overcommits the cache

items.title: PagedAttention: block tables and prefix sharing
items.purpose: Show the OS-paging analogy and the prefix-sharing win it unlocks.
items.description: Fixed-size blocks allocated on demand bound waste to one partial block per sequence — and because blocks are referenced, sequences sharing a system prompt share its compute.

flow.title: Partition memory into blocks
flow.detail: Each block holds the KV entries for a fixed number of tokens.

flow.title: Map through a block table
flow.detail: Each sequence maps logical token positions to physical blocks, exactly like page tables.

flow.title: Allocate as you grow
flow.detail: Memory tracks tokens actually generated rather than max_tokens reserved.

flow.title: Share a prefix by reference
flow.detail: Sequences with the same system prompt point at the same blocks with a refcount.

flow.title: Copy on write
flow.detail: Blocks are copied only when the sequences diverge.

numbers.label: Naive waste
numbers.detail: Reserved-but-unused memory plus fragmentation in contiguous allocation.

numbers.label: Block size
numbers.detail: Bounds internal fragmentation to one partial block per sequence.

tradeoffs: Requires a custom attention kernel that understands block tables
Adds an indirection per attention access
Copy-on-write costs a copy exactly when sequences diverge

items.title: Why one long prompt stalls everyone else
items.purpose: Make the cross-request interference visible, since it is invisible in fleet dashboards.
items.description: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. Mixed in one step, a single 8K-token prompt becomes every other user’s visible stutter.

flow.title: A long prompt arrives
flow.detail: An 8K-token prefill enters the same batch as streaming users.

flow.title: The step goes compute-bound
flow.detail: Prefill saturates the matrix units for a long step.

flow.title: Decode stalls behind it
flow.detail: Every streaming user waits, and their TPOT spikes for reasons they did not cause.

flow.title: Chunk the prefill
flow.detail: Splitting the prompt and interleaving with decode keeps any single step short.

flow.title: Or disaggregate
flow.detail: Separate GPU pools for prefill and decode, shipping the KV cache between them.

numbers.label: Prompt spread
numbers.detail: Prefill cost scales with prompt length; decode does not.

numbers.label: Decode parallelism
numbers.detail: No parallelism within a sequence — only across sequences in the batch.

tradeoffs: Chunking adds scheduling complexity
Disaggregation needs a fast interconnect to ship the KV cache
Overload shows as slower tokens, not errors — dashboards look healthy

design-problems/p23.title: RAG / Semantic Search visual study set
design-problems/p23.summary: Four sheets separate the two-pipeline map from the three decisions that set answer quality: chunking, hybrid two-stage retrieval, and embedding-model migration.

items.title: RAG system map
items.purpose: Show that ingest and query are separate pipelines joined only by the index.
items.description: Documents are chunked, embedded and indexed once; queries embed, retrieve, rerank and ground the model. The embedding model is the schema shared by both halves.

flow.title: Chunk the corpus
flow.detail: Split on structure with overlap so no answer is cut at a boundary.

flow.title: Embed and index
flow.detail: Store vectors plus ACL tags, document id and a content hash for incremental re-ingest.

flow.title: Retrieve on query
flow.detail: Embed the query, search lexically and semantically, pre-filter by permission.

flow.title: Rerank
flow.detail: A cross-encoder scores query-passage pairs jointly and keeps the best few.

flow.title: Ground and cite
flow.detail: The model answers only from retrieved passages and returns provenance.

numbers.label: Corpus
numbers.detail: About 40M chunks at roughly four chunks per document.

numbers.label: Index size
numbers.detail: 768-dimension float32; near 30 GB after int8 quantization.

numbers.label: Retrieval budget
numbers.detail: So generation, not retrieval, dominates end-to-end latency.

priorities: Citations and provenance end to end
tradeoffs: Bigger chunks give context but dilute the embedding
ANN buys speed by giving up recall
Fresher indexes cost continuous re-embedding

items.title: Chunking and parent-document retrieval
items.purpose: Make the precision-versus-context tension concrete and show the technique that resolves it.
items.description: An embedding is one fixed-size vector, so a large chunk averages ideas into a vague point and a small one lacks context. Match on the small chunk, return the large one.

flow.title: Split on structure
flow.detail: Headings and sections beat fixed size when the corpus has shape.

flow.title: Overlap the edges
flow.detail: Roughly 50 tokens of overlap stops an answer being severed at a boundary.

flow.title: Prepend context
flow.detail: Document title and section path travel with each chunk.

flow.title: Match small
flow.detail: Embedding and search operate on the precise child chunk.

flow.title: Return the parent
flow.detail: The model receives the larger section the match came from.

numbers.label: Chunk size
numbers.detail: Baseline before structure-aware splitting.

numbers.label: Overlap
numbers.detail: Cheap insurance against boundary loss.

tradeoffs: Small chunks match precisely but lack context
Large chunks carry context but blur the vector
Overlap raises index size and duplicate hits

items.title: Two-stage hybrid retrieval
items.purpose: Explain why retrieval splits into a cheap recall stage and an expensive precision stage.
items.description: Bi-encoders can be precomputed but never see the pair; cross-encoders read the pair but cannot be precomputed. So recall about 100 cheaply, then rerank to about five.

flow.title: Embed the query
flow.detail: One small forward pass, roughly 10 milliseconds.

flow.title: Search both ways
flow.detail: ANN for meaning, BM25 for rare literal tokens such as error codes.

flow.title: Fuse the rankings
flow.detail: Reciprocal rank fusion merges two ordered lists into one.

flow.title: Rerank the survivors
flow.detail: A cross-encoder scores each query-passage pair jointly.

flow.title: Apply a relevance floor
flow.detail: If nothing clears it, answer "I do not know" rather than grounding on noise.

numbers.label: Recall stage
numbers.detail: Optimised for not missing the answer.

numbers.label: Precision stage
numbers.detail: What actually reaches the context window.

priorities: Not missing the answer at stage one
tradeoffs: Cross-encoders are accurate but cannot be indexed
Wider candidate sets cost rerank latency
Post-filtering permissions leaks through counts and timing

items.title: Migrating the embedding model
items.purpose: Show why an embedding upgrade is a schema migration rather than a config change.
items.description: Vectors from two models occupy different spaces, so a new query against an old index returns nonsense rather than degraded results. Dual-index and gate the cutover on quality.

flow.title: Stand up index B
flow.detail: Build alongside A rather than in place.

flow.title: Dual-write on ingest
flow.detail: New documents land in both indexes so B stays current.

flow.title: Backfill the corpus
flow.detail: Re-embed everything, at a cost estimated up front rather than discovered.

flow.title: Gate on quality
flow.detail: Compare A and B on a fixed evaluation set before moving traffic.

flow.title: Cut over, keep A warm
flow.detail: Rollback must stay cheap because regressions surface late.

numbers.label: Backfill cost
numbers.detail: 40M chunks at roughly 1000 chunks per second per GPU.

numbers.label: Rollback window
numbers.detail: Quality regressions are often noticed a day later.

tradeoffs: Dual indexes double storage during migration
Backfill competes with live ingest for GPUs
Cutting over early risks an unmeasured regression

design-problems/p30.title: Feature Store visual study set
design-problems/p30.summary: Four sheets separate the dual-store map from the three things that decide whether a model behaves the same in production as in training.

items.title: Feature store system map
items.purpose: Establish that one registered definition compiles into both materialization paths.
items.description: A feature is declared once and compiled to a batch path and a streaming path, landing in a low-latency online store for inference and a full-history offline store for training.

flow.title: Register the definition
flow.detail: Entity, source, transformation, freshness TTL and target stores, all versioned.

flow.title: Compile to both paths
flow.detail: The same definition drives the batch job and the stream processor.

flow.title: Materialize online
flow.detail: Current values only, keyed by entity, for single-digit-millisecond reads.

flow.title: Materialize offline
flow.detail: Full history with timestamps, stored columnar for large temporal joins.

flow.title: Serve both consumers
flow.detail: Inference reads online by key; training reads offline as of a label time.

numbers.label: Online footprint
numbers.detail: 50M entities by 200 features at roughly 50 bytes.

numbers.label: Online latency
numbers.detail: It sits inside the model request path.

numbers.label: Inference load
numbers.detail: Fetched as one row per entity, not 200 separate gets.

priorities: Online latency inside the request budget
tradeoffs: Two stores mean two materialization paths to keep honest
Streaming freshness costs continuous compute
Materializing every feature for every entity wastes storage

items.title: Point-in-time correctness
items.purpose: Show exactly which feature value a training row is allowed to contain.
items.description: A training row may only use values knowable at its label timestamp. Using a later value teaches the model to rely on information it will never have at prediction time.

flow.title: Start from label rows
flow.detail: Entity id, label timestamp and label, potentially hundreds of millions of rows.

flow.title: Keep feature history
flow.detail: Every value stored with the event timestamp it became valid.

flow.title: Join as-of, backward
flow.detail: Take the latest value at or before the label timestamp.

flow.title: Bound with a TTL
flow.detail: Without one, a row happily matches a value from a year earlier.

flow.title: Sort-merge at scale
flow.detail: Both sides stream past each other once instead of per-row lookups.

numbers.label: Join type
numbers.detail: Not a key join — the timestamp is the whole point.

numbers.label: Failure mode
numbers.detail: Excellent backtest, broken production model.

priorities: Reproducible output for the same inputs
Event time distinguished from processing time
tradeoffs: Temporal joins cost far more than key lookups
Longer history improves training and grows storage
Tight TTLs drop valid rows, loose ones admit stale values

items.title: Where training/serving skew comes from
items.purpose: Name the silent failure the whole system exists to prevent.
items.description: Two implementations of one definition drift at the edges — timezones, cancellations, null handling — so the model receives a different distribution than it trained on.

flow.title: Feature defined once
flow.detail: A single logical definition, for example a 30-day average order value.

flow.title: Reimplemented twice
flow.detail: Batch SQL in a notebook, live computation in the serving path.

flow.title: Edges disagree
flow.detail: Timezone boundaries, cancelled orders, inclusive or exclusive windows, nulls.

flow.title: Distributions diverge
flow.detail: Serving inputs no longer match what the model learned.

flow.title: Fix structurally
flow.detail: Compile both paths from one definition so no second implementation exists.

numbers.label: Symptom
numbers.detail: The most common cause of a model that validates and then fails.

numbers.label: Direct test
numbers.detail: Recompute offline what was served online for the same entity and time.

priorities: One source of truth per feature
tradeoffs: Structural fixes cost more up front than a quick reimplementation
Continuous skew checks consume compute
Statistical fixes such as regularization address a different failure

items.title: Per-feature freshness and missing values
items.purpose: Show that freshness is declared per feature and that a missing value must be explicit.
items.description: A 30-day average tolerates hours of staleness; a session click count tolerates seconds. A missing value must be a flagged default, never a silent zero.

flow.title: Declare a TTL
flow.detail: Freshness is a property of the feature, not of the system.

flow.title: Serve if fresh
flow.detail: Value within TTL is returned normally.

flow.title: Expire if stale
flow.detail: Past TTL, serve the default and raise a staleness alert.

flow.title: Default if absent
flow.detail: Cold-start entities get a documented default plus a was-defaulted flag.

flow.title: Log what was served
flow.detail: The served vector is both the debugging record and the skew baseline.

numbers.label: Batch features
numbers.detail: Slow-moving aggregates and demographics.

numbers.label: Streaming features
numbers.detail: Session and last-N-minutes counters.

priorities: Alerting on staleness before accuracy drops
tradeoffs: Streaming freshness costs continuous compute
Short TTLs raise default rates
Logging every served vector adds storage

design-problems/p31.title: Content Moderation visual study set
design-problems/p31.summary: Four sheets separate the cascade map from the three decisions that make the system workable: threshold bands, overload triage, and the reviewer feedback loop.

items.title: Moderation pipeline system map
items.purpose: Show the cheap-first cascade and the three-way routing decision.
items.description: Hash matching runs before any model, the publish decision splits by stakes, and scores route three ways. The architecture decides what a human never has to see.

flow.title: Match known-bad hashes
flow.detail: Exact and perceptual hashes catch re-uploads in microseconds.

flow.title: Split by stakes
flow.detail: Catastrophic categories block before publish; the rest publish and scan asynchronously.

flow.title: Run the cascade
flow.detail: Cheap text and image classifiers first, large multimodal models only on survivors.

flow.title: Route on score
flow.detail: Auto-remove above the high threshold, auto-approve below the low one, review between.

flow.title: Enforce and record
flow.detail: Apply the action and write an audit record with a policy reason code.

numbers.label: Volume
numbers.detail: About 1,150 per second average, designed for 5K peak.

numbers.label: Review load
numbers.detail: Roughly 8,300 reviewer-hours daily, over 1,000 full-time reviewers.

numbers.label: Cascade order
numbers.detail: Microseconds, then milliseconds, then hundreds of milliseconds.

priorities: Reviewer attention spent only where needed
tradeoffs: Blocking pre-publish protects users but delays every post
Publishing optimistically is fast but leaves harm briefly live
Larger models are more accurate and far more expensive

items.title: Two thresholds, not one
items.purpose: Show why a single cut-off is the wrong shape for this problem.
items.description: One threshold turns every borderline item into an automated error. A band converts model uncertainty into the one resource that can resolve it — human judgement.

flow.title: Calibrate the score
flow.detail: An uncalibrated 0.8 is not a probability, and thresholds mean nothing without calibration.

flow.title: Set the high cut-off
flow.detail: Above it, auto-remove without review.

flow.title: Set the low cut-off
flow.detail: Below it, auto-approve without review.

flow.title: Route the band
flow.detail: Between them, send to a human — where the model knows least.

flow.title: Tune per category
flow.detail: Child safety favours recall; spam favours precision.

numbers.label: Band width
numbers.detail: Halving the uncertain band halves a thousand-person operation.

numbers.label: False-positive signal
numbers.detail: Without appeals the false-positive rate is unobservable.

priorities: Error ratio owned jointly with policy
tradeoffs: Favouring recall raises review cost
Favouring precision leaves more harm live
Recalibration after a model update silently shifts every threshold

items.title: Triage when the queue exceeds capacity
items.purpose: Show why arrival order is the worst possible allocation under overload.
items.description: FIFO treats a viral threat identically to a three-view meme. Ranking by severity times predicted reach puts scarce human attention where damage accrues fastest.

flow.title: Measure the overflow
flow.detail: Arrival exceeds review capacity, so something must be dropped or deferred.

flow.title: Score expected harm
flow.detail: Severity multiplied by predicted reach from follower count and early velocity.

flow.title: Review the top slice
flow.detail: Human attention goes to the highest-damage items first.

flow.title: Apply an explicit tail policy
flow.detail: Auto-action conservatively or expire with an audit record.

flow.title: Alert on queue age
flow.detail: Age percentiles reveal starvation that queue length hides.

numbers.label: Arrival
numbers.detail: Against a review capacity of 1M per day.

numbers.label: Overflow
numbers.detail: Needs a stated policy, not silent accumulation.

tradeoffs: Priority ranking starves low-severity items by design
Auto-actioning the tail raises false positives
Expiring the tail leaves some harm unreviewed

items.title: The reviewer feedback loop and its failure modes
items.purpose: Show what the loop buys and the three ways it degrades.
items.description: Reviewer decisions are labels from exactly where the model is weakest, which is active learning by construction — and also a biased sample that automates reviewer bias at scale.

flow.title: Humans decide the band
flow.detail: Every review produces a label plus a policy reason code.

flow.title: Labels feed retraining
flow.detail: The uncertain band narrows, cutting review cost over time.

flow.title: Correct sampling bias
flow.detail: Label a random sample too, or the training set only reflects the band.

flow.title: Audit for bias
flow.detail: Golden sets and per-group error rates catch reviewer bias before it is automated.

flow.title: Red-team the blind spots
flow.detail: The model never learns about content it never surfaced.

numbers.label: Retraining cadence
numbers.detail: Adversaries adapt continuously, so a static model degrades by design.

numbers.label: Agreement metric
numbers.detail: Low agreement means the policy is ambiguous, not that reviewers are careless.

priorities: Labels where the model is weakest
Bias detected before it is automated
Coverage of what the model never surfaces
tradeoffs: Band-only labels are an unrepresentative sample
Reviewer bias becomes uniform, invisible model bias
Multi-review improves labels and consumes scarce capacity

design-problems/p26.title: Observability Platform visual study set
design-problems/p26.summary: Four sheets separate the three-store map from the things that actually decide whether the platform survives: cardinality, compression, and cross-signal correlation.

items.title: Observability platform system map
items.purpose: Show why three signals need three stores behind one ingest path.
items.description: Metrics, logs and traces have conflicting access patterns — range reads, filtered scans and graph assembly — so they share ingest and diverge at storage.

flow.title: Collect at the host
flow.detail: Agents batch locally and never block the application thread.

flow.title: Validate and quota
flow.detail: The gateway enforces per-tenant limits before anything reaches storage.

flow.title: Buffer durably
flow.detail: A queue absorbs storage restarts so ingest never back-pressures production.

flow.title: Split by signal
flow.detail: Time series, log objects and spans land in stores shaped for their reads.

flow.title: Query and alert
flow.detail: Dashboards and alert rules read metrics; investigation crosses all three.

numbers.label: Metric points
numbers.detail: 10M active series scraped every 15 seconds.

numbers.label: Log volume
numbers.detail: About 58 MB/sec sustained — the storage cost driver.

numbers.label: Spans unsampled
numbers.detail: 100K requests/sec at roughly 20 spans each.

tradeoffs: Three stores cost more to operate than one
Durable buffering adds delivery latency
Sampling saves money and loses detail

items.title: Why cardinality, not volume, kills metrics
items.purpose: Name the single most common way a metrics system falls over.
items.description: A series is identified by its full label set, so one unbounded label creates one series per value — and the label index is memory-resident, so it fails hard rather than degrading.

flow.title: Start with a normal metric
flow.detail: A request counter with roughly 100 series.

flow.title: Add a bounded label
flow.detail: Status code with five values gives 500 series — entirely fine.

flow.title: Add an unbounded label
flow.detail: User id with a million values gives 100 million series.

flow.title: Watch the index grow
flow.detail: The label-to-series index lives in memory and grows without bound.

flow.title: Fail hard
flow.detail: Out-of-memory kills and query timeouts hit every tenant on the node.

numbers.label: Safe label
numbers.detail: Status, method, region — small closed sets.

numbers.label: Unsafe label
numbers.detail: User id, request id, session id, full URL path.

priorities: Cardinality visible as a first-class metric
Blast radius contained to one tenant
tradeoffs: Quotas protect the cluster and reject some legitimate metrics
High-cardinality data still needs a home in logs or traces
Rejecting at ingest loses data that cannot be recovered

items.title: Delta-of-delta and XOR compression
items.purpose: Explain why the highest-volume signal is also the cheapest to store.
items.description: Timestamps arrive at near-fixed intervals and values change slowly, so a 16-byte pair compresses to one or two bytes.

flow.title: Store the first point
flow.detail: A full timestamp and value anchor the series.

flow.title: Delta the timestamps
flow.detail: Then store only the change in delta — zero for a regular scrape.

flow.title: XOR the values
flow.detail: Similar floats share leading and trailing bits, so only the middle window is stored.

flow.title: Chunk by time window
flow.detail: The current chunk is in memory behind a write-ahead log; closed chunks are immutable.

flow.title: Downsample the old
flow.detail: Five-minute and hourly rollups keep long-range queries cheap.

numbers.label: Raw point
numbers.detail: A timestamp plus a float64.

numbers.label: Compressed point
numbers.detail: Which is why 670K points/sec is only about 115 GB/day.

items.description: Verification is a local signature check inside the calling service, so auth must be available for login and refresh — not for every request.

flow.title: Authenticate once
flow.detail: Credentials plus MFA, verified against a slow salted hash.

flow.title: Create a session
flow.detail: A durable record of this login on this device.

flow.title: Issue two credentials
flow.detail: A short stateless access token and a long revocable refresh token.

flow.title: Verify locally
flow.detail: Any service checks the signature against a cached public key set.

flow.title: Refresh periodically
flow.detail: Only the refresh call ever touches the auth service.

numbers.label: Password hash
numbers.detail: Slow by design, which makes login CPU-bound.

numbers.label: Verification
numbers.detail: A local signature check, costing auth nothing.

numbers.label: Without stateless tokens
numbers.detail: What every-request verification would cost.

priorities: Verification off the auth critical path
tradeoffs: Stateless verification cannot be revoked directly
Cached key sets must tolerate a JWKS outage
Login capacity is CPU planning, not I/O planning

items.title: The tension the two-token split resolves
items.purpose: Make the central tradeoff explicit before presenting the solution.
items.description: Statelessness is what makes verification free and revocation impossible, so the two properties belong on two different credentials.

flow.title: Want free verification
flow.detail: A self-contained signed token needs no lookup.

flow.title: Discover the cost
flow.detail: There is nothing to change, so it cannot be revoked.

flow.title: Want instant revocation
flow.detail: A lookup per request gives complete control.

flow.title: Discover that cost too
flow.detail: It reintroduces the round trip the token avoided.

flow.title: Split the credential
flow.detail: Short stateless access token, long stateful refresh token.

numbers.label: Access token TTL
numbers.detail: This is the revocation latency.

numbers.label: Refresh token
numbers.detail: Opaque, stored hashed, presented only to auth.

priorities: Sensitive state kept off the hot path
tradeoffs: Shorter TTLs revoke faster and increase refresh traffic
Longer TTLs cut traffic and widen the theft window
A denylist restores immediacy at per-request cost

items.title: Refresh rotation and reuse detection
items.purpose: Show how theft becomes detectable rather than silent.
items.description: Each refresh issues a new token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token is usable at most once and its reuse is a signal.

flow.title: Present the refresh token
flow.detail: The only call that reaches the auth service in steady state.

flow.title: Issue a new pair
flow.detail: A fresh access token and a fresh refresh token.

flow.title: Invalidate the old one
flow.detail: The previous refresh token is now single-use and spent.

flow.title: Detect reuse
flow.detail: A spent token reappearing means someone is replaying it.

flow.title: Kill the family
flow.detail: Revoke every token in the chain and force re-login.

numbers.label: Reuse detections
numbers.detail: A spike here is the earliest warning available.

numbers.label: Storage
numbers.detail: A raw refresh token store is as sensitive as a password store.

priorities: Blast radius limited to one token family
tradeoffs: Rotation can false-positive across concurrent regions
Killing a family logs out a legitimate user too
More rotation means more refresh traffic

items.title: Rotating the signing key without logging everyone out
items.purpose: Show why the overlap window is the whole mechanism.
items.description: Both keys must verify for at least the lifetime of the longest outstanding token, or rotation becomes a fleet-wide forced logout.

flow.title: Publish both keys
flow.detail: The key set contains the old and new keys together.

flow.title: Let verifiers refresh
flow.detail: Services fetch and cache the set before anything changes.

flow.title: Sign with the new key
flow.detail: Tokens carry a key id so verifiers select correctly.

flow.title: Wait out the overlap
flow.detail: Old-key tokens remain valid until they expire naturally.

flow.title: Retire the old key
flow.detail: Only once no outstanding token depends on it.

numbers.label: Overlap window
numbers.detail: Retiring early invalidates live tokens.

numbers.label: Key id
numbers.detail: What makes multi-key verification possible at all.

priorities: A break-glass path for key compromise
Verifiers that tolerate a stale key set
tradeoffs: Overlap means a compromised old key stays valid briefly
Symmetric signing would require sharing the secret everywhere
Cached key sets delay awareness of a new key
